claims.text: High-entropy alloys with optimized grain-boundary structure and composition will exhibit an improved combination of strength, ductility, Young's modulus, and fracture resistance.
As-cast or wrought high-entropy alloys have random grain-boundary structures and compositions.
Thermomechanical processing can engineer the grain-boundary structure of high-entropy alloys.
Optimization of alloying elements can engineer grain-boundary composition in high-entropy alloys.
The proposed effect should hold for processing temperatures from 800 to 1200 °C.
The proposed effect should hold for strain rates from 10^-3 to 10^-1 s^-1.
The proposed effect should hold for equiatomic or near-equiatomic alloys containing four to six principal elements.
Grain-boundary engineering promotes beneficial precipitate formation.
Enhanced grain-boundary cohesion, reduced impurity segregation, and beneficial precipitate formation lead to improved mechanical properties.
The intervention will increase strength by 10–20% relative to state-of-the-art high-entropy alloys.
The intervention will improve ductility by 15–30% relative to state-of-the-art high-entropy alloys.
The intervention will increase Young's modulus by 5–10% relative to state-of-the-art high-entropy alloys.
The intervention will enhance fracture resistance by 20–50% relative to state-of-the-art high-entropy alloys.
State-of-the-art high-entropy alloys have random grain-boundary structures and compositions.
The proposed effect should not hold outside the specified processing-temperature or strain-rate ranges.
The proposed effect should not hold for alloys containing fewer than four or more than six principal elements.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome specifies improvements in all four targeted properties, but the falsification rule permits the hypothesis to survive when only two properties improve. Thus, failure of one or two of the explicit quantitative predictions may not falsify the hypothesis.
